claim: During pathological aggregation, proteins undergo remarkable conformational re-arrangements to anomalously assemble into a heterogeneous collection of misfolded multimers, ranging from soluble oligomers to insoluble amyloid fibrils.
source: During pathological aggregation, proteins undergo remarkable conformational re-arrangements to anomalously assemble into a heterogeneous collection of misfolded multimers, ranging from soluble oligomers to insoluble amyloid fibrils.
evidence: This is a general statement about protein aggregation that draws from established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The sequence segments spanning helices α2 and α3 underwent a compaction during the formation of OL.
source: The sequence segments spanning helices α2 and α3 underwent a compaction during the formation of OL and elongation into β-sheets during the formation of OS.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET measurements and kinetic modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The sequence segments spanning helices α2 and α3 underwent elongation into β-sheets during the formation of OS.
source: The sequence segments spanning helices α2 and α3 underwent a compaction during the formation of OL and elongation into β-sheets during the formation of OS.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET measurements and kinetic modeling presented in the manuscript.

claim: The β1-α1-β2 and α2-α3 subdomains were separated in both OL and OS.
source: The β1-α1-β2 and α2-α3 subdomains were separated, and the helix α1 was unfolded to varying extents in both OL and OS.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET measurements showing changes in distance between subdomains.

claim: The helix α1 was unfolded to varying extents in both OL and OS.
source: The β1-α1-β2 and α2-α3 subdomains were separated, and the helix α1 was unfolded to varying extents in both OL and OS.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET measurements showing decreased FRET efficiency for the W144-C153 pair.

claim: The mostly α-helical and monomeric prion protein (PrP) undergoes drastic secondary and tertiary structural re-arrangements upon aggregation into a variety of misfolded β-sheet-rich multimers.
source: The mostly α-helical and monomeric prion protein (PrP) undergoes drastic secondary and tertiary structural re-arrangements upon aggregation into a variety of misfolded β-sheet-rich multimers (Pan et al., 1993), most of which are not infectious.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pan et al., 1993.

claim: Most misfolded β-sheet-rich multimers of PrP are not infectious.
source: The mostly α-helical and monomeric prion protein (PrP) undergoes drastic secondary and tertiary structural re-arrangements upon aggregation into a variety of misfolded β-sheet-rich multimers (Pan et al., 1993), most of which are not infectious.
evidence: This is stated as a fact following the citation to Pan et al., 1993.

claim: A class of fatal neurodegenerative diseases collectively known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies are caused by infectious aggregates of misfolded PrP.
source: A class of fatal neurodegenerative diseases collectively known as transmissible spongiform encephalopathies are caused by infectious aggregates of misfolded PrP.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about prion diseases.

claim: Conversion to the pathogenic form of PrP possibly initiates in the endocytic pathway, when the protein encounters an acidic environment.
source: Conversion to the pathogenic form possibly initiates in the endocytic pathway, when the protein encounters an acidic environment (Borchelt et al., 1992).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Borchelt et al., 1992.

claim: The most infectious oligomers of PrP are composed of 14–28 monomers.
source: The pathogenic misfolded aggregates thus formed in vivo are highly heterogeneous, with the most infectious oligomers composed of 14–28 monomers (Silveira et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Silveira et al., 2005.

claim: The pathogenic misfolded aggregates of PrP formed in vivo are highly heterogeneous.
source: The pathogenic misfolded aggregates thus formed in vivo are highly heterogeneous, with the most infectious oligomers composed of 14–28 monomers (Silveira et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Silveira et al., 2005.

claim: A major section of the β-rich core of the aggregates formed from the full length PrP is located in the sequence segment that corresponds to the α2-α3 subdomain of monomeric PrP.
source: While some models suggest that a major part of the native fold remains intact in the aggregates (DeMarco and Daggett, 2004; Govaerts et al., 2004), several experimental studies have shown that a major section of the β-rich core of the aggregates formed from the full length PrP is located in the sequence segment that corresponds to the α2-α3 subdomain of monomeric PrP (Cobb et al., 2007; Diaz-Espinoza and Soto, 2012; Singh et al., 2012; Tycko et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to experimental studies.

claim: The oligomerization and misfolding of mouse PrP (moPrP) is favoured in vitro at low pH in the presence of 150 mM NaCl.
source: In agreement with observations made in vivo, the oligomerization and misfolding of mouse PrP (moPrP) is favoured in vitro at low pH in the presence of 150 mM NaCl (Singh et al., 2014; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015b), due to the protonation of residues H186 and/or D201 in the α2-α3 subdomain of moPrP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2014 and Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015b.

claim: The oligomerization and misfolding of moPrP at low pH is due to the protonation of residues H186 and/or D201 in the α2-α3 subdomain.
source: In agreement with observations made in vivo, the oligomerization and misfolding of mouse PrP (moPrP) is favoured in vitro at low pH in the presence of 150 mM NaCl (Singh et al., 2014; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015b), due to the protonation of residues H186 and/or D201 in the α2-α3 subdomain of moPrP.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2014 and Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015b.

claim: The protected core region of the β-rich oligomers formed by PrP at low pH in vitro resembles that of amyloid fibrils derived from diseased brain.
source: Previous HX-MS studies (Singh et al., 2012; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a) had shown that the protected core region of the β-rich oligomers formed by PrP at low pH in vitro resembles that of amyloid fibrils derived from diseased brain.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to HX-MS studies.

claim: Recombinant PrP from animal species with high susceptibility to prion disease readily forms β-rich oligomers at low pH in vitro.
source: Not surprisingly then, recombinant PrP from animal species with high susceptibility to prion disease has been shown to readily form β-rich oligomers at low pH in vitro (Khan et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Khan et al., 2010.

claim: β-rich oligomers formed at low pH readily disrupt lipid membranes.
source: β-rich oligomers formed at low pH, readily disrupt lipid membranes; this property is a likely reason for their toxicity (Singh et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2014 and Singh et al., 2012.

claim: The ability to disrupt lipid membranes is a likely reason for the toxicity of β-rich oligomers formed at low pH.
source: β-rich oligomers formed at low pH, readily disrupt lipid membranes; this property is a likely reason for their toxicity (Singh et al., 2014; Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on the membrane disruption property.

claim: Oligomer formation of moPrP at pH 4 could be completely abolished by substituting the TVTTTT sequence stretch in the C-terminal end of α2 with AAAAAA.
source: Interestingly, oligomer formation of moPrP at pH 4 could be completely abolished by substituting a discordant but highly conserved sequence stretch (TVTTTT) in the C-terminal end of α2, with a very high β-sheet propensity (Dima and Thirumalai, 2002), by the α-helix favouring residue alanine (AAAAAA) (Singh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2014.

claim: The C-terminal end of α2 plays a critical role in the initiation of misfolding of moPrP.
source: This suggests that the C-terminal end of α2 plays a critical role in the initiation of misfolding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that substituting the TVTTTT sequence abolishes oligomer formation.

claim: In species with low susceptibility to prion disease, the loop between β2 and α2 is more rigid in the monomeric prion protein.
source: In species with low susceptibility to prion disease, the loop between β2 and α2 is more rigid in the monomeric prion protein (Gossert et al., 2005), suggesting that its flexibility might play an important role in facilitating misfolding.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Gossert et al., 2005.

claim: The flexibility of the loop between β2 and α2 might play an important role in facilitating misfolding.
source: In species with low susceptibility to prion disease, the loop between β2 and α2 is more rigid in the monomeric prion protein (Gossert et al., 2005), suggesting that its flexibility might play an important role in facilitating misfolding.
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation about loop rigidity in low-susceptibility species.

claim: Residues H186 and D201 together with R155, K193 and E195 form a network of electrostatic interactions between the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains in monomeric PrP.
source: It is also known that residues H186 and D201 together with R155, K193 and E195 form a network of electrostatic interactions between the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains in monomeric PrP (Hadži et al., 2015; Hosszu et al., 2010; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015b).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The disruption of electrostatic interactions between the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains by lowering pH and adding salt facilitates misfolding and oligomer formation in vitro.
source: The disruption of these electrostatic interactions either by a lowering of pH (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016a) and addition of salt (Sengupta et al., 2017), or by charge reversing or neutralizing pathogenic mutations (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016a; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a) facilitate misfolding and oligomer formation in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Charge reversing or neutralizing pathogenic mutations facilitate misfolding and oligomer formation in vitro.
source: The disruption of these electrostatic interactions either by a lowering of pH (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016a) and addition of salt (Sengupta et al., 2017), or by charge reversing or neutralizing pathogenic mutations (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016a; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a) facilitate misfolding and oligomer formation in vitro.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations.

claim: Separation of the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains must occur before conversion to the β-conformation.
source: It appears that separation of the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains must occur before conversion to the β-conformation (Eghiaian et al., 2007; Hafner-Bratkovic et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Eghiaian et al., 2007 and Hafner-Bratkovic et al., 2011.

claim: Locking of the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains by engineering in an artificial disulphide bond prevents misfolding and aggregation.
source: Locking of the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains either by engineering in an artificial disulphide bond (Eghiaian et al., 2007), or by binding to anti-prion drugs (Kamatari et al., 2013) prevent misfolding and aggregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Eghiaian et al., 2007.

claim: Binding to anti-prion drugs prevents misfolding and aggregation of PrP.
source: Locking of the α2-α3 and β1-α1-β2 subdomains either by engineering in an artificial disulphide bond (Eghiaian et al., 2007), or by binding to anti-prion drugs (Kamatari et al., 2013) prevent misfolding and aggregation.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kamatari et al., 2013.

claim: Real-time NMR measurements showed that no major conformational change occurs in the monomer before it assembles into oligomer.
source: Real-time NMR measurements had shown that no major conformational change occurs in the monomer before it assembles into oligomer: the monomer structure is perturbed to only a very minor extent before assembly into oligomers, which is rate-limited by association steps in which dimers and trimers are formed (Sengupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sengupta et al., 2017.

claim: The monomer structure is perturbed to only a very minor extent before assembly into oligomers.
source: Real-time NMR measurements had shown that no major conformational change occurs in the monomer before it assembles into oligomer: the monomer structure is perturbed to only a very minor extent before assembly into oligomers, which is rate-limited by association steps in which dimers and trimers are formed (Sengupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sengupta et al., 2017.

claim: Assembly into oligomers is rate-limited by association steps in which dimers and trimers are formed.
source: Real-time NMR measurements had shown that no major conformational change occurs in the monomer before it assembles into oligomer: the monomer structure is perturbed to only a very minor extent before assembly into oligomers, which is rate-limited by association steps in which dimers and trimers are formed (Sengupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sengupta et al., 2017.

claim: Misfolded monomeric PrP is not stable.
source: Not surprisingly, single-molecule studies have found that misfolded monomeric PrP is not stable (Yu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yu et al., 2012.

claim: Oligomerization is faster than major conformational change in two pathogenic mutant variants of moPrP.
source: Measurements of changes in size and conformation by CD (circular dichroism), SEC (size-exclusion chromatography) and HX-MS (hydrogen-exchange coupled to mass spectrometry), had shown that oligomerization is faster than major conformational change in the case of two pathogenic mutant variants of moPrP (Sabareesan and Udgaonkar, 2016), under oligomerization conditions identical to those used in the current study.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sabareesan and Udgaonkar, 2016.

claim: β-rich oligomers of moPrP form worm-like fibrils by an isodesmic mechanism at pH 2.
source: Notably, β-rich oligomers of moPrP, which form worm-like fibrils by an isodesmic mechanism at pH 2 (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008), are distinct from the off-pathway oligomers seen to form transiently during nucleation-dependent amyloid fibril formation (Sabareesan and Udgaonkar, 2017), from the octamers formed at low pH in the presence of 2 M urea (Larda et al., 2013), from the oligomers formed spontaneously by a tandem dimer (Gilch et al., 2003), and from the neurotoxic oligomers obtained by thermal refolding of ovine prion protein (Eghiaian et al., 2007; Rezaei et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008.

claim: The Trp-TNB FRET pair has an estimated Forster radius (R0) of ~23 Å.
source: The Trp-TNB FRET pair has an estimated Forster radius (R0) of ~23 Å (Supplementary file 1), which allows the reliable measurement of change in distance in the range of ~11 to ~35 Å (Lakshmikanth et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Supplementary file 1 and a citation to Lakshmikanth et al., 2001.

claim: The Trp-TNB FRET pair allows the reliable measurement of change in distance in the range of ~11 to ~35 Å.
source: The Trp-TNB FRET pair has an estimated Forster radius (R0) of ~23 Å (Supplementary file 1), which allows the reliable measurement of change in distance in the range of ~11 to ~35 Å (Lakshmikanth et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lakshmikanth et al., 2001.

claim: WT moPrP has eight Trp residues, seven of which are located in the intrinsically disordered N terminal region (NTR), and one (W144) at the N terminus of α1 in the structured C-terminal domain (CTD).
source: WT moPrP has eight Trp residues, seven of which are located in the intrinsically disordered N terminal region (NTR), and one (W144) at the N terminus of α1 in the structured C-terminal domain (CTD).
evidence: This is a factual statement about the structure of WT moPrP.

claim: All native Trp residues are solvent-exposed in the WT moPrP monomer.
source: All native Trp residues are solvent-exposed in the WT moPrP monomer.
evidence: This is a factual statement about the structure of WT moPrP monomer.

claim: The NTR remains disordered in the oligomer.
source: The NTR remains disordered in the oligomer, and major structural changes take place in the CTD upon oligomerization (Sengupta et al., 2017; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sengupta et al., 2017 and Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a.

claim: Major structural changes take place in the CTD upon oligomerization.
source: The NTR remains disordered in the oligomer, and major structural changes take place in the CTD upon oligomerization (Sengupta et al., 2017; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sengupta et al., 2017 and Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a.

claim: The fluorescence emission maximum was at 355 nm for monomeric mutant variants with W144 as the donor fluorophore.
source: The fluorescence emission maximum was at 355 nm and 345 nm, for monomeric mutant variants with W144 and W197 as the donor fluorophore, respectively (Figure 1B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence emission spectra shown in Figure 1B-F.

claim: The fluorescence emission maximum was at 345 nm for monomeric mutant variants with W197 as the donor fluorophore.
source: The fluorescence emission maximum was at 355 nm and 345 nm, for monomeric mutant variants with W144 and W197 as the donor fluorophore, respectively (Figure 1B–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence emission spectra shown in Figure 1B-F.

claim: W144 is completely exposed to solvent in the solution NMR structure of monomeric moPrP.
source: This observation, indicating a markedly different local environment around each Trp residue, is in agreement with the solution NMR structure of monomeric moPrP, where W144 is completely exposed to solvent, and W197 is partially buried (Riek et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riek et al., 1996.

claim: W197 is partially buried in the solution NMR structure of monomeric moPrP.
source: This observation, indicating a markedly different local environment around each Trp residue, is in agreement with the solution NMR structure of monomeric moPrP, where W144 is completely exposed to solvent, and W197 is partially buried (Riek et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Riek et al., 1996.

claim: In the TNB-labelled monomeric mutant variants, the Trp fluorescence was quenched, but to different extents.
source: In the corresponding TNB-labelled monomeric mutant variants, the Trp fluorescence was quenched, but to different extents.
evidence: This is observed from the fluorescence emission spectra in Figure 1.

claim: The extent of quenching by TNB was dependent on the separation of the Trp and the TNB moiety in the monomer.
source: The extent of quenching by TNB was dependent on the separation of the Trp and the TNB moiety in the monomer, clearly indicative of FRET.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed quenching patterns.

claim: The observed FRET efficiencies for different pairs of mutant variants were in good agreement with the expected FRET efficiencies calculated from the solution NMR structure.
source: In addition, the observed FRET efficiencies for different pairs of mutant variants were in good agreement with the expected FRET efficiencies calculated from the solution NMR structure (Figure 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of observed and calculated FRET efficiencies.

claim: The far-UV CD spectra of all unlabelled and TNB-labelled mutant variants matched well with that of WT moPrP.
source: Moreover, the far-UV CD spectra of all unlabelled and TNB-labelled mutant variants matched well with that of WT moPrP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that the secondary structure is conserved in these proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by CD spectra shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The secondary structure is conserved in all unlabelled and TNB-labelled mutant variants.
source: Moreover, the far-UV CD spectra of all unlabelled and TNB-labelled mutant variants matched well with that of WT moPrP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), indicating that the secondary structure is conserved in these proteins.
evidence: This is an inference based on the CD spectra matching WT moPrP.

claim: All the unlabelled and TNB-labelled mutant variants were able to form β-rich oligomers, comparable to those formed by WT moPrP.
source: While all the unlabelled and TNB-labelled mutant variants were able to form β-rich oligomers, comparable to those formed by WT moPrP as judged by CD and DLS measurements (Sengupta and Udgaonkar, 2017), (Figure 1—figure supplement 2), the local environment around donor fluorophores W144 and W197 changed in different ways upon oligomer formation.
evidence: This claim is supported by CD and DLS measurements and a citation.

claim: A blue shift to 345 nm and an increase in quantum yield was observed for the W144-containing mutant variants upon oligomer formation.
source: A blue shift to 345 nm and an increase in quantum yield was observed for the W144-containing mutant variants, suggesting that the local environment of W144 was more hydrophobic in the oligomers than in the monomer (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence emission spectra shown in Figure 1D-F.

claim: The local environment of W144 was more hydrophobic in the oligomers than in the monomer.
source: A blue shift to 345 nm and an increase in quantum yield was observed for the W144-containing mutant variants, suggesting that the local environment of W144 was more hydrophobic in the oligomers than in the monomer (Figure 1D–F).
evidence: This is an inference based on the blue shift and increased quantum yield.

claim: A slightly decreased quantum yield without a change in the emission maximum was observed for the W197-containing mutant variants upon oligomer formation.
source: In contrast, a slightly decreased quantum yield without a change in the emission maximum was observed for the W197-containing mutant variants (Figure 1B–C) indicating that the W197 side-chain was partially buried in both monomer and oligomer, but that additional quenching mechanisms were operative in the oligomer.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence emission spectra shown in Figure 1B-C.

claim: The W197 side-chain was partially buried in both monomer and oligomer.
source: In contrast, a slightly decreased quantum yield without a change in the emission maximum was observed for the W197-containing mutant variants (Figure 1B–C) indicating that the W197 side-chain was partially buried in both monomer and oligomer, but that additional quenching mechanisms were operative in the oligomer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence data.

claim: Additional quenching mechanisms were operative in the oligomer for W197-containing mutant variants.
source: In contrast, a slightly decreased quantum yield without a change in the emission maximum was observed for the W197-containing mutant variants (Figure 1B–C) indicating that the W197 side-chain was partially buried in both monomer and oligomer, but that additional quenching mechanisms were operative in the oligomer.
evidence: This is an inference based on the decreased quantum yield in oligomers.

claim: The enhanced FRET efficiency in the oligomers compared to the monomers, in all five mutant variants, suggested that both intra- and inter-molecular FRET could be contributing to the quenching of the tryptophan fluorescence in the oligomers.
source: The enhanced FRET efficiency in the oligomers compared to the monomers, in all five mutant variants, suggested that both intra- and inter-molecular FRET could be contributing to the quenching of the tryptophan fluorescence in the oligomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enhanced FRET efficiency in oligomers.

claim: The FRET efficiencies were similar for the oligomers prepared at 1:34 (~3 mol%) and 1:50 (2 mol%) doping ratios.
source: The FRET efficiencies were similar for the oligomers prepared at 1:34 (~3 mol%) and 1:50 (2 mol%) doping ratios (Figure 2A), and significantly lower than that determined for oligomers prepared from the dopant protein alone (i.e. without Trp-less moPrP), or for oligomers prepared at a 1:13 (~8 mol%) doping ratio.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET efficiency measurements shown in Figure 2A.

claim: At doping ratios greater than ~1:30, inter-molecular FRET was effectively suppressed.
source: The data suggested that at doping ratios greater than ~1:30, inter-molecular FRET was effectively suppressed.
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET efficiency data at different doping ratios.

claim: The moPrP oligomers formed at pH 4 have a molecular weight of 1207 ± 165 kDa from MALS measurements.
source: The moPrP oligomers formed at pH 4 are comparable to the β-sheet rich oligomers at pH 2 (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008) (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2010) (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2011), with a molecular weight of 1207 ± 165 kDa from MALS measurements (Singh et al., 2012), corresponding to ~53 ± 7 monomeric units.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2012.

claim: The moPrP oligomers formed at pH 4 correspond to ~53 ± 7 monomeric units.
source: The moPrP oligomers formed at pH 4 are comparable to the β-sheet rich oligomers at pH 2 (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2008) (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2010) (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2011), with a molecular weight of 1207 ± 165 kDa from MALS measurements (Singh et al., 2012), corresponding to ~53 ± 7 monomeric units.
evidence: This is calculated from the molecular weight measurement.

claim: The global misfolding kinetics at 1:50 and 1:99 doping ratios were indistinguishable from that of only Trp-less moPrP.
source: The global misfolding kinetics at 1:50 and 1:99 doping ratios were indistinguishable from that of only Trp-less moPrP.
evidence: This claim is supported by CD-monitored misfolding kinetics data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Only slightly faster kinetics was observed at 1:5 and 1:10 doping ratios compared to Trp-less moPrP alone.
source: Only slightly faster kinetics was observed at 1:5 and 1:10 doping ratios (Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Supplementary file 3.

claim: At a doping ratio of 1:50, the dopant protein and Trp-less moPrP did not oligomerize independently of each other.
source: To conclusively demonstrate that at a doping ratio of 1:50, the dopant protein and Trp-less moPrP did not oligomerize independently of each other, or that the oligomerization kinetics of Trp-less moPrP was altered, 2 μM dopant protein was mixed with 98 μM Trp-less protein, and the oligomerization reaction was monitored by steady-state Trp fluorescence anisotropy (Figure 2C and Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by steady-state Trp fluorescence anisotropy measurements shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Although 100 μM TNB-labelled W197-C223 by itself misfolded more than fourfold faster than 100 μM TNB labelled W144-C153, the kinetics measured by steady-state fluorescence anisotropy was the same when either was used as dopant at the 1:50 doping ratio.
source: Although 100 μM TNB-labelled W197-C223 by itself misfolded more than fourfold faster than 100 μM TNB labelled W144-C153 (Supplementary file 2), the kinetics measured by steady-state fluorescence anisotropy was the same, no matter which of them was used as dopant at the 1:50 doping ratio.
evidence: This claim is supported by steady-state fluorescence anisotropy measurements and data in Supplementary file 2.

claim: The kinetics of co-oligomerization at 1:50 doping ratio was comparable to the kinetics of CD-monitored misfolding of 100 μM Trp-less moPrP by itself.
source: Moreover, the kinetics was comparable to the kinetics of CD-monitored misfolding of 100 μM Trp-less moPrP by itself.
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of kinetics data.

claim: At 2 μM concentration, either dopant protein by itself is expected to oligomerize with an apparent rate constant of <0.02 h−1.
source: Furthermore, at 2 μM concentration, either dopant protein by itself is expected to oligomerize with an apparent rate constant of <0.02 h−1, from the known dependence of the oligomerization rate of moPrP on protein concentration (Sabareesan and Udgaonkar, 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on the known concentration dependence of oligomerization rate, supported by a citation.

claim: The apparent rate constant from steady state Trp fluorescence anisotropy measurement was 0.1 h−1.
source: The observation that the apparent rate constant from steady state Trp fluorescence anisotropy measurement was 0.1 h−1, indicated that this probe reported on the co-oligomerization of dopant protein and Trp-less moPrp, and not on the independent oligomerization of 2 μM dopant protein.
evidence: This claim is supported by steady-state Trp fluorescence anisotropy measurements.

claim: The fluorescence spectra of the native monomers of the different unlabelled and labelled moPrP variants differed from those of the corresponding misfolded oligomers.
source: The fluorescence spectra of the native monomers of the different unlabelled and labelled moPrP variants differed from those of the corresponding misfolded oligomers (Figure 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence spectra shown in Figure 1.

claim: There was no measurable change in fluorescence accompanying the misfolding and oligomerization of Trp-less moPrP by itself.
source: Since there was no measurable change in fluorescence accompanying the misfolding and oligomerization of Trp-less moPrP by itself (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), the fluorescence change accompanying co-oligomerization of 2 μM dopant protein with 98 μM Trp-less moPrP, was easily measurable.
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: 2 µM dopant protein alone (in the absence of Trp-less moPrP) under oligomerization conditions did not undergo any conformation-sensitive change in Trp fluorescence in ~30 hrs.
source: 2 µM dopant protein alone (in the absence of Trp-less moPrP) under oligomerization conditions did not undergo any conformation-sensitive change in Trp fluorescence in ~30 hrs (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: When the dopant was present at 2 mol%, the kinetics of conformational change was not dependent on whether the dopant was labelled with TNB or not.
source: Thus, when the dopant was present at 2 mol%, the kinetics of conformational change was not dependent on whether the dopant was labelled with TNB or not.
evidence: This is an inference based on the fluorescence-monitored kinetics data.

claim: Trp-less moPrP was found to form two populations of oligomers, the larger OL and the smaller OS, at pH 4 and 150 mM NaCl.
source: In agreement with previous results obtained with WT moPrP (Singh et al., 2014), Trp-less moPrP was found to form two populations of oligomers, the larger OL and the smaller OS, at pH 4 and 150 mM NaCl, As oligomerization progressed, the total amount of oligomers increased, but the sizes (as estimated from their elution volumes) remained fixed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 3B and a citation.

claim: As oligomerization progressed, the total amount of oligomers increased, but the sizes remained fixed.
source: In agreement with previous results obtained with WT moPrP (Singh et al., 2014), Trp-less moPrP was found to form two populations of oligomers, the larger OL and the smaller OS, at pH 4 and 150 mM NaCl, As oligomerization progressed, the total amount of oligomers increased, but the sizes (as estimated from their elution volumes) remained fixed (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The kinetics of monomer loss/oligomer formation were found to be apparently single exponential in nature, with a characteristic time (1/k) of 16.7 ± 2.8 hr.
source: The kinetics of monomer loss/oligomer formation, as determined from the SEC measurements, were found to be apparently single exponential in nature, with a characteristic time (1/k) of 16.7 ± 2.8 hr (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by SEC measurements shown in Figure 3C.

claim: The populations of M and of OL and OS together were estimated to be ~14% and ~86%, respectively, after 60 hr of oligomerization.
source: The populations of M and of OL and OS together were estimated to be ~14% and ~86%, respectively, after 60 hr of oligomerization.
evidence: This is estimated from SEC data.

claim: OS was populated to about a threefold higher extent than was OL at equilibrium.
source: The poor resolution of the SEC column made it difficult to reliably estimate the relative amounts of OL and OS at equilibrium, but it appeared that, OS was populated to about a threefold higher extent than was OL.
evidence: This is an estimate from SEC data with acknowledged uncertainty.

claim: The co-oligomerization of the three unlabelled mutant variants containing W144 with Trp-less moPrP was accompanied by a slow ~80% increase in fluorescence in a single kinetic phase.
source: Here, the co-oligomerization of the three unlabelled mutant variants containing W144 (W144-C153, W144-C199 and W144-C223) with Trp-less moPrP was accompanied by a slow ~80% increase in fluorescence in a single kinetic phase with characteristic times (1/k) of 8.3 ± 1.3, 6.7 ± 2.7 and 10 ± 1 hr, respectively (Figure 4A–C and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4A-C and Table 1.

claim: The two unlabelled mutant moPrP variants containing W197 underwent a quenching of fluorescence in two kinetic phases: a burst phase change (~40% amplitude) which was complete within the dead time of measurement (5 min), and a slow phase which accounted for the rest of the signal change (~60% amplitude).
source: In marked contrast to the W144 variants, the two unlabelled mutant moPrP variants containing W197 (W197-C169 and W197-C223) underwent a quenching of fluorescence in two kinetic phases: a burst phase change (~40% amplitude) which was complete within the dead time of measurement (5 min), and a slow phase which accounted for the rest of the signal change (~60% amplitude) during the co-oligomerization reaction (Figure 4D–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence measurements shown in Figure 4D-E.

claim: The characteristic times for the slow kinetic phase of W197-C169 and W197-C223 were 8.3 ± 0.7 and 8.3 ± 2.1 hr.
source: The characteristic times for the slow kinetic phase were 8.3 ± 0.7 and 8.3 ± 2.1 hr (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The characteristic times of the slow phase of fluorescence change for the different W144 and W197 mutant variants were comparable, and depended on the total protein concentration.
source: The characteristic times of the slow phase of fluorescence change for the different W144 and W197 mutant variants were comparable, and depended on the total protein concentration (while keeping the doping ratio fixed at 1:50), as expected for an assembly reaction (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: When a doping ratio of 1:99 was used, the characteristic times remained unchanged for both the unlabelled W144-C153 and W197-C223 mutant variants.
source: In contrast, when a doping ratio of 1:99 was used (while keeping the total protein concentration fixed), the characteristic times remained unchanged for both the unlabelled W144-C153 and W197-C223 mutant variants (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: The burst phase change in Trp fluorescence was complete before co-oligomer formation had commenced.
source: First, the amplitude of the burst phase change in Trp fluorescence was comparable for both the unlabelled and labelled proteins, indicating that no change in intra-molecular FRET efficiency occurred in the dead time of measurement. This further confirmed that the burst-phase change in fluorescence reflected only a localized perturbation to the environment of W197, before oligomerization commenced.
evidence: This is an inference based on the amplitude of the burst phase change.

claim: The FRET efficiency changed in two observable kinetic phases for W197-C169 and W197-C223: a fast phase during which intra-molecular FRET efficiency increased and a slow phase during which it decreased.
source: Second, the FRET efficiency changed in two observable kinetic phases: a fast phase during which intra-molecular FRET efficiency increased and a slow phase during which it decreased.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRET measurements shown in Figure 4.

claim: The apparent fast compaction of the sequence segments spanning both α2 and α3 appeared to take place with characteristic times of 1.7 ± 0.2 and 1.4 ± 0.3 hr for W197-C169 and W197-C223, respectively.
source: The apparent fast compaction of the sequence segments spanning both α2 and α3, as seen in the increase in FRET efficiency, appeared to take place with characteristic times of 1.7 ± 0.2 and 1.4 ± 0.3 hr, respectively (Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The characteristic times for the slow phase of elongation/FRET decrease were 16.7 ± 2.8 and 11.1 ± 2.5 hr for W197-C169 and W197-C223, respectively.
source: The characteristic times for the slow phase of elongation/FRET decrease (16.7 ± 2.8 and 11.1 ± 2.5 hr) were comparable to the characteristic time of global misfolding, as monitored by far-UV CD (11.1 ± 3.7 hr) (Figure 3A and Table 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Table 1.

claim: The characteristic times for the slow phase of elongation/FRET decrease were comparable to the characteristic time of global misfolding, as monitored by far-UV CD.
source: The characteristic times for the slow phase of elongation/FRET decrease (16.7 ± 2.8 and 11.1 ± 2.5 hr) were comparable to the characteristic time of global misfolding, as monitored by far-UV CD (11.1 ± 3.7 hr) (Figure 3A and Table 1).
evidence: This is a comparison of characteristic times from different measurements.

claim: The sequential M ↔ OL ↔ OS model correctly predicted the monomer loss kinetics determined from SEC, the concentrations of M, OL and OS at the end of 60 hr, and the experimentally observed FRET-monitored kinetics.
source: The parallel OS ↔ M ↔ OL model and the sequential M ↔ OS ↔ OL model could not satisfy all three criteria adequately, but the sequential M ↔ OL ↔ OS model could do so.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic modeling and global fitting of SEC and FRET data.

claim: M oligomerizes reversibly to form OL with a characteristic time (1/k) of 11.1 hr.
source: This model predicted that M oligomerizes reversibly to form OL, which then disaggregates reversibly to form OS, with characteristic times (1/k) for the M → OL, OL → M, OL → OS and OS → OL transitions, of 11.1, 20, 11.1 and 33.3 hr, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic modeling.

claim: OL disaggregates reversibly to M with a characteristic time (1/k) of 20 hr.
source: This model predicted that M oligomerizes reversibly to form OL, which then disaggregates reversibly to form OS, with characteristic times (1/k) for the M → OL, OL → M, OL → OS and OS → OL transitions, of 11.1, 20, 11.1 and 33.3 hr, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic modeling.

claim: OL disaggregates reversibly to form OS with a characteristic time (1/k) of 11.1 hr.
source: This model predicted that M oligomerizes reversibly to form OL, which then disaggregates reversibly to form OS, with characteristic times (1/k) for the M → OL, OL → M, OL → OS and OS → OL transitions, of 11.1, 20, 11.1 and 33.3 hr, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic modeling.

claim: OS converts reversibly to OL with a characteristic time (1/k) of 33.3 hr.
source: This model predicted that M oligomerizes reversibly to form OL, which then disaggregates reversibly to form OS, with characteristic times (1/k) for the M → OL, OL → M, OL → OS and OS → OL transitions, of 11.1, 20, 11.1 and 33.3 hr, respectively.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic modeling.

claim: For the sequence segments 197–169 and 197–223, the FRET efficiency values are higher in OL than in OS.
source: Global fitting of all the FRET data further predicted that (i) for the sequence segments 197–169 and 197–223, the FRET efficiency values are higher in OL than in OS, and that (ii) for the 144–153 and 144–199 segments, the FRET efficiency values are lower in OL and OS than in M (Figure 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by global fitting of FRET data shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: For the 144–153 and 144–199 segments, the FRET efficiency values are lower in OL and OS than in M.
source: Global fitting of all the FRET data further predicted that (i) for the sequence segments 197–169 and 197–223, the FRET efficiency values are higher in OL than in OS, and that (ii) for the 144–153 and 144–199 segments, the FRET efficiency values are lower in OL and OS than in M (Figure 5 and Table 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by global fitting of FRET data shown in Figure 5 and Table 2.

claim: At pH 4 and 7, ΔG of WT moPrP has been reported to be 4.6 and 6.04 kcal mol−1 respectively.
source: At pH 4 and 7, ΔG has been reported to be 4.6 and 6.04 kcal mol−1 respectively.
evidence: This is stated as a known fact about WT moPrP stability.

claim: While misfolding/oligomerization is 100% complete within 24 hr at pH 4, it is only ~5% complete at pH 5.7 on the same timescale.
source: Moreover, it has been shown that while misfolding/oligomerization is 100% complete within 24 hr at pH 4, it is only ~5% complete at pH 5.7 on the same timescale (Singh et al., 2014; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Singh et al., 2014 and Singh and Udgaonkar, 2016a.

claim: At pH 7, moPrP forms amyloid fibrils, and oligomers are either completely absent or present in undetectable amounts.
source: It should be noted that at pH 7, moPrP forms amyloid fibrils, and that oligomers are either completely absent or present in undetectable amounts (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh and Udgaonkar, 2013.

claim: Previous real-time NMR measurements had not detected any major structural rearrangement in the monomer, prior to oligomerization at pH 4 in the presence of 150 mM NaCl.
source: Previous real-time NMR measurements had not detected any major structural rearrangement in the monomer, prior to oligomerization at pH 4 in the presence of 150 mM NaCl.
evidence: This refers to previous NMR measurements.

claim: The burst-phase change in fluorescence for W197-containing mutant variants is likely a consequence of a local change in monomeric moPrP before the start of oligomerization, namely the disruption of the K193-E195 salt-bridge in the α2-α3 loop.
source: This is likely a consequence of a local change in monomeric moPrP before the start of oligomerization, namely the disruption of the K193-E195 salt-bridge in the α2-α3 loop, in accordance with previous NMR measurements (Sengupta et al., 2017).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Sengupta et al., 2017.

claim: The secondary structure and size of the Trp-less moPrP oligomers were found to be comparable to that of WT moPrP.
source: The secondary structure and size (as estimated from CD and DLS measurements, respectively) (Sengupta and Udgaonkar, 2017) of the Trp-less moPrP oligomers were found to be comparable to that of WT moPrP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD and DLS measurements and a citation.

claim: Trp-less moPrP misfolded and oligomerized ~2.5 fold slower compared to that of WT moPrP.
source: However, Trp-less moPrP misfolded and oligomerized ~2.5 fold slower compared to that of WT moPrP (Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Supplementary file 2.

claim: A compaction of the segments spanning the α2 and α3 helices is the fastest change during oligomerization.
source: A qualitative comparison of the characteristic times of all structural changes monitored by FRET suggests that a compaction of the segments spanning the α2 and α3 helices is the fastest change (Table 1).
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of characteristic times in Table 1.

claim: The slowest changes appeared to be the unfolding of α1, and the expansion of the sequence segments that encompassed α2 and α3 into extended β-strands.
source: The slowest changes appeared to be the unfolding of α1, and the expansion of the sequence segments that encompassed α2 and α3 into extended β-strands.
evidence: This is an inference based on comparison of characteristic times.

claim: The slow decrease in FRET efficiency in α1 is likely to be due to the unfolding of this helix.
source: The slow decrease in FRET efficiency in α1 is likely to be due to the unfolding of this helix (Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a).
evidence: This is an inference supported by a citation to Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a.

claim: Domain separation occurs spontaneously under acidic conditions which mimic the endocytic environment in the cell.
source: Remarkably, these results suggest that domain separation occurs spontaneously under acidic conditions which mimic the endocytic environment in the cell, in marked contrast to previous results where oligomerization was induced by thermal denaturation (Eghiaian et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an inference based on the FRET results, contrasted with previous results.

claim: It is possible to directly show that the β1-α1-β2 sub-domain separates from the α2-α3 subdomain during the formation of the misfolded oligomers, by using an appropriately placed FRET donor-acceptor pair.
source: Moreover, this study shows that it is possible to directly show that the β1-α1-β2 sub-domain separates from the α2-α3 subdomain during the formation of the misfolded oligomers, by using an appropriately placed FRET donor-acceptor pair.
evidence: This is a methodological claim based on the results of this study.

claim: The elongation of sequence segments that had spanned α2 and α3 is possibly due to their conversion into β-sheets.
source: The slowest change appears to be the elongation of sequence segments that had spanned α2 and α3; this is possibly due to their conversion into β-sheets and is also reported on by the global probe CD (Figure 6).
evidence: This is speculation based on the FRET and CD data.

claim: The sequence segment spanning α3 appears to undergo a fast compaction and a slow elongation, as does the sequence segment spanning α2.
source: From the FRET measurements reported here, the sequence segment spanning α3 appears to undergo a fast compaction and a slow elongation, as does the sequence segment spanning α2.
evidence: This is an inference based on FRET measurements.

claim: HX-MS experiments could not detect any significant conformational change in the α3 segment upon oligomer formation.
source: In contrast, HX-MS experiments could not detect any significant conformational change in this segment upon oligomer formation: α3 was found to be highly protected against HX in both the monomer and oligomer (Sabareesan and Udgaonkar, 2016; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to HX-MS studies.

claim: α3 was found to be highly protected against HX in both the monomer and oligomer.
source: In contrast, HX-MS experiments could not detect any significant conformational change in this segment upon oligomer formation: α3 was found to be highly protected against HX in both the monomer and oligomer (Sabareesan and Udgaonkar, 2016; Singh and Udgaonkar, 2015a).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to HX-MS studies.

claim: HX-MS fails to detect conformational changes in α3 which might be taking place concomitant to oligomer formation because α3 is part of the buried core of both the monomer and the oligomer.
source: Since α3 is part of the buried core of both the monomer and the oligomer, HX-MS fails to detect conformational changes which might be taking place in α3, concomitant to oligomer formation.
evidence: This is an explanation for the apparent discrepancy between HX-MS and FRET results.

claim: FRET can detect structural changes in α3 readily during oligomer formation.
source: FRET, on the other hand, can detect these structural changes readily.
evidence: This is a claim about the capability of FRET based on the results.

claim: EPR studies at neutral pH on disulfide-free mutant variants of the PrP in nanodiscs suggested that α1 and α3 retain their helicity, and that only α2 undergoes conversion to the β-conformation.
source: Importantly, these results are in contrast to EPR studies carried out at neutral pH, on disulfide-free mutant variants of the PrP in nanodiscs, which had suggested that α1 and α3 retain their helicity, and that only α2 undergoes conversion to the β-conformation (Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yang et al., 2015.

claim: OL can disaggregate into OS.
source: The observations from the SEC experiments that both large (OL) and small (OS) oligomers are formed sequentially from monomer M, and that both oligomers and monomer coexist at equilibrium at pH 4 in the presence of 150 mM NaCl, along with the previous demonstration that OL can disaggregate into OS (Jain and Udgaonkar, 2010) allowed kinetic modelling of the SEC data according to a M ↔ OL ↔ OS mechanism.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jain and Udgaonkar, 2010.

claim: The formation of OL from M is accompanied by compaction of the sequence segments spanning the α2 and α3 helices.
source: Hence, the kinetic modelling indicates that the structural changes accompanying oligomerization occur in two steps. The formation of OL from M is accompanied by compaction of the sequence segments spanning the α2 and α3 helices, which accounts for the higher FRET efficiency seen for sequence segments 197–169 and 197–223 in OL.
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic modeling and FRET data.

claim: The subsequent dissociation of OL to OS is accompanied by an expansion of the sequence segments spanning α2 and α3.
source: The subsequent dissociation of OL to OS is accompanied by an expansion of the same sequence segments, which is likely to be due to the formation of extended β-sheet structure in OS.
evidence: This is an inference based on kinetic modeling and FRET data.

claim: The expansion of sequence segments spanning α2 and α3 during OL to OS transition is likely to be due to the formation of extended β-sheet structure in OS.
source: The subsequent dissociation of OL to OS is accompanied by an expansion of the same sequence segments, which is likely to be due to the formation of extended β-sheet structure in OS.
evidence: This is speculation based on the FRET data.

claim: It is possibly the formation of β-sheet structure that makes OS more stable than OL.
source: It is possibly the formation of β-sheet structure that makes OS more stable than OL.
evidence: This is speculation based on the structural changes observed.

claim: The sequence stretch 190–197 spanning a segment of the α2 helix and the α2-α3 loop is weakly protected in OL, but moderately protected in OS.
source: These observations are supported by previous HX-MS measurements of the oligomers at pH 2 which showed that the sequence stretch 190–197 spanning a segment of the α2 helix and the α2- α3 loop is weakly protected in OL, but moderately protected in OS, suggesting that the α2 helix is unstructured in OL, but may have converted to β-sheet in OS (Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Singh et al., 2012.

claim: The α2 helix is unstructured in OL, but may have converted to β-sheet in OS.
source: These observations are supported by previous HX-MS measurements of the oligomers at pH 2 which showed that the sequence stretch 190–197 spanning a segment of the α2 helix and the α2- α3 loop is weakly protected in OL, but moderately protected in OS, suggesting that the α2 helix is unstructured in OL, but may have converted to β-sheet in OS (Singh et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference based on HX-MS measurements, supported by a citation.

claim: The α1 helix is weakly protected in OL, but moderately protected in OS.
source: Moreover, the α1 helix is weakly protected in OL, but moderately protected in OS in accordance with the FRET results.
evidence: This is stated as being in accordance with FRET results.

claim: For an α-helix to convert into a β-sheet, intra-helical hydrogen bonds must be disrupted, for new inter-strand hydrogen bonds to form.
source: For an α-helix to convert into a β-sheet, intra-helical hydrogen bonds must be disrupted, for new inter-strand hydrogen bonds to form.
evidence: This is established knowledge about protein structural transitions.

claim: Helices must undergo partial or complete unfolding before they can re-arrange their hydrogen bond structure to form β-sheets.
source: It has been suggested that helices must undergo partial or complete unfolding before they can re-arrange their hydrogen bond structure to form β-sheets (Ding et al., 2003; Qin and Buehler, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ding et al., 2003 and Qin and Buehler, 2010.

claim: The presence of highly dynamic and frustrated sequence segments like the TVTTTT stretch at the C terminal end of α2 possibly aids the early partial unfolding/compaction.
source: The presence of highly dynamic and frustrated sequence segments like the TVTTTT stretch at the C terminal end of α2, possibly aids the early partial unfolding/compaction (Chen and Thirumalai, 2013).
evidence: This is speculation supported by a citation to Chen and Thirumalai, 2013.

claim: The disulphide bond stapling α2 and α3 might be a deterrent to complete unfolding, but could be crucial in positioning the two helices in an optimal position for inter-strand hydrogen bond formation.
source: On the other hand, the disulphide bond stapling α2 and α3 might be a deterrent to complete unfolding, but could be crucial in positioning the two helices in an optimal position for inter-strand hydrogen bond formation.
evidence: This is speculation about the role of the disulfide bond.

claim: Folding simulations of α-helix formation have detected misfolded β-hairpin like structures and compact structures with non-native hydrogen bonds.
source: Indeed, folding simulations of α-helix formation have detected misfolded β-hairpin like structures and compact structures with non-native hydrogen bonds (Bertsch et al., 1998; Lin et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bertsch et al., 1998 and Lin et al., 2014.

claim: The data presented is the first real-time experimental demonstration of the sequence of segment-specific conformational changes that occur in each monomeric unit of moPrP as it forms oligomers.
source: In conclusion, the data presented here is the first real-time experimental demonstration of the sequence of segment-specific conformational changes that occur in each monomeric unit of moPrP as it forms oligomers.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study.
